title: Leading a team is a design problem
subtitle: Building a design function — and what I changed when collaboration kept breaking down in one working relationship
team: Team of five, including a design lead

sections.headline: Leading a team is a design problem
sections.subtext: As Head of Product Design at a B2B SaaS platform company I had a team of five, a seat at the leadership table, and a design practice to turn into a real function. The part I think about most was none of that. It was a working relationship that kept breaking down, and how long it took me to look in the right place.

sections.headline: The role
sections.content:
I joined to make design a real function. The company was in the middle of a platform shift, and design needed to carry the same weight as product and engineering rather than sit downstream of them.

Most of that was the expected work. I managed a team of five, including a design lead. I built a planning process so design, product, and engineering worked from the same picture. I set up shared governance of the design system across four designers and engineering. I hired people, and when someone was not the right fit, I made that call too.

The part that taught me the most was not on that list.

sections.quote: When collaboration breaks down, the first question is 'what is wrong with our system?', not 'what is wrong with that person?'
sections.context: The reframe at the centre of how I lead

sections.headline: Where collaboration kept breaking down
sections.content:
The work of one senior engineer was not landing with the rest of the team. Meetings were tense. Points got cut off before they were finished. Over time the team learned to route around the collaboration rather than work through it.

It did not add up. The engineering work itself was excellent, and the ideas, once there was room for them, were often the sharpest in the room.

I tried the conventional moves first. Feedback about how contributions were landing. Smaller meetings. Clearer expectations. None of it changed anything — and it should not have. Every one of those moves put the cost of the problem on one person and left the process that produced it completely untouched. That was my mistake, and I made it for longer than I would like.

So I stopped assessing a person and started recording conditions. When did this collaboration fail, and when did it work? The pattern was consistent. It failed in fast group discussion, on questions asked cold, and under time pressure. It worked one to one, in writing, and whenever the material had gone out in advance. Same person, same capability, opposite outcomes — the variable was the setting, not the individual.

Our collaboration ran on a single default: fast, verbal, loudest voice first. Nobody had chosen that default on purpose, which is exactly why nobody was accountable for what it filtered out.

steps.label: Agendas, shared early
steps.description: Every meeting got a written agenda in advance. No more "quick syncs" that turned into hour-long debates no one could prepare for.

steps.label: Room to prepare
steps.description: Context and material went out before group discussions, so thinking could happen ahead of the meeting rather than under time pressure inside it.

steps.label: Turn-taking, on purpose
steps.description: In group settings I made space for sequential input, instead of letting whoever spoke loudest set the outcome.

steps.label: Decisions in writing
steps.description: Important decisions were written down, not left to whoever remembered the conversation their way.

steps.label: Coaching the design lead
steps.description: I coached my design lead through the same shift — how to set up the conditions for a strained engineering relationship and work through it directly, rather than routing around it.

sections.headline: The pushback
sections.content:
Not everyone agreed at first. "Why should we change how we work for one person?" — sometimes asked out loud, sometimes through eye-rolls and foot-dragging.

My answer was that we were not changing it for one person. We were changing it because the process had a bias we had never examined: it rewarded speed of response over quality of thinking, and we had no idea what that was costing us.

I also made the plain business case. Good ideas were being filtered out before they were heard. That is a cost, not just a fairness question. And the changes were cheap — an agenda, material sent ahead, a decision written down.

sections.headline: What changed

metrics.label: The collaboration
metrics.before: Tension, points dismissed, the team routing around the working relationship
metrics.after: Contributions landed and got airtime, and problems got caught earlier

metrics.label: Team norms
metrics.after: Written agendas, prep time, and documented decisions became how the team worked by default

metrics.label: How the team thought about friction
metrics.value: People started asking what was wrong with the process before deciding what was wrong with a person

sections.narrative: Within months the dynamic shifted. The bigger change was that the structured habits spread. Other people adopted the prep, the agendas, and the written decisions for themselves — they stopped being a fix for one situation and became the norm. The same attention I gave to one set of working conditions is the attention I give to product design: understand the real need, design for the edge case, check the assumption.

sections.headline: What I took from it
sections.content:
Good leadership is not mainly about managing people. It is about designing the conditions people work within. When collaboration breaks down, look at the system before you look at the person — and notice how much more comfortable it is to do the reverse.

And you cannot build inclusive software with an exclusive team process. Human-centred teams are what make human-centred products possible.

executive.summary: Built a design function from the ground up — a team of five, a design system, a seat at the leadership table. Defining example: diagnosed why one collaboration kept failing, redesigned how the team worked, and turned lost contribution into some of the team's strongest.

blog.summary: When collaboration keeps breaking down, the instinct is to manage the person. But what if the problem is not the person — it is how the team is designed to work?
blog.angle: Designing team collaboration around how people actually work
